What are some books to learn about social systems in general, learn about socialism specifically, and get some biased perspectives from figures who believe in either socialism or another social system strongly?
What are some good books to read about socialism?
A People's History of the United States by Howard Zinn

The only socialist book I enjoyed reading was Looking Backward by Bellamy.
Cool. I'll look into it once I read a few nonfiction books!

I'd recommend Animal Farm by George Orwell as a first introduction to socialism. It's a thinly veiled critique of Stalinism, but it shows all of the benefits that come from socialism and the dangers of a power vacuum created along the way. It's also wonderfully short; if you read often it will probably only take you a day to read the entirety of the novel. Then read the Wealth Of Nations (in it's entirety) if you haven't done that yet. Adam Smith is often wrongly accused of promoting full Laissez-Faire Capitalism, but he was way too smart for that. Most of his magnum opus is concerned with the dangers of Capitalism as a system while still demonstrating how much better it is than the mercantilism that preceeded it. Das Kapital by Karl Marx is the far more relevant work of Marx to read if you want to understand socialism, and is in huge part a response to the Wealth of nations. After Das Kapital it's really up to you what aspects of socialism appeal to you, but those three books are hugely and I mean HUGELY influential on socialist thought, and pretty much everything else is derivative from them.

I read Animal Farm on a whim a few summers ago and I think I just went through it too fast and remember almost nothing and didn't understand a lot of it. I may re-read it. I'll definitely check out those others! Thank you for the very well spoken and detailed response!

Adam Smith is often wrongly accused of promoting full Laissez-Faire Capitalism, but he was way too smart for that. Most of his magnum opus is concerned with the dangers of Capitalism as a system while still demonstrating how much better it is than the mercantilism that preceeded it.

^^^This! I hate how the most vociferous proponents of capitalism clearly have no idea that the neoliberal ideologies that they promote go against the most fundamental principles of capitalist thought espoused by Smith in Wealth Of Nations.

Life at the Bottom: The Worldview That Makes the Underclass by Theodore Dalrymple, is an account of British underclass life that generations of socialist policies have created. Required reading for anyone interested in the welfare state.
Economics in One Lesson by Henry Hazlitt

What kind of socialism are you looking into? If you're looking at utopian or state socialism, Marx and Engles are excellent starting points, anything written by them will be good. Robert Owen is also an important name in utopian socialism, though drifting more toward syndicalism. I personally lean more towards anarchist socialism, and I just finished the memoirs of Kropotkin, which was excellent. Of course Mikhail Bakunin is probably the biggest name in anarchism so check him out if that sort of thing is up your alley. If you are interested in getting an American perspective, Emma Goldman is highly recommended, as is Alexander Berkman. The labor leaders of the late 19th and early 20th century certainly had more socialist tendencies than their counterparts today, though that would definately be more along the syndicalist line of thinking. You could check out Samuel Gompers and the heads of other big unions like The Knights of Labor, The IWW, The CIO, The UMW, etc. Hope this helps!
